newsitem.title: USA: Job worry effect on wages only temporary--S.F. Fed.
newsitem.headline: Job worry effect on wages only temporary--S.F. Fed.

text.p: Worker anxiety about possible job loss may have helped hold down wage demands, but the effect is likely to be small and temporary, a new study by the San Francisco Federal Reserve Bank said on Wednesday.
The study, by economist Rob Valletta, concluded that recent national concerns about corporate downsizing, job displacement and job security appear to be well-founded.
But it also argued that those trends have been concentrated among skilled, white-collar workers and thus should not have a big, long-lasting impact on the economy.
"Given ... the small percentage of the work force who experience displacement, any wage moderating effects of job insecurity are likely to be small," Valletta said.
"Any moderating effects," he added, "are likely to be temporary," thanks to a generally strong labor market.

Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan argued last month that a big reason for America's good inflation performance was subdued wage demands by workers worried about losing their jobs due to corporate downsizing and other structural changes.
But he said that could only last for so long and saw signs that the period of subdued wage growth might be coming to an end.
